newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says U.S. raids weakened Saddam, met goals.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says U.S. raids weakened Saddam, met goals.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday that this week's cruise missile attacks against Iraq had further weakened President Saddam Hussein and accomplished immediate U.S. goals.
But he reserved the right to strike again after Iraqi forces twice challenged a newly expanded no-fly zone in southern Iraq designed to make it harder for Saddam to threaten oil-rich Gulf states.

"The air strikes, the missile strikes, that were conducted over the last few days have been successful," Clinton told reporters. "The targets are either destroyed or sufficiently damaged so that you can say that our mission has been achieved."
In defying the White House, Iraq sent two MiG fighters toward U.S. warplanes before turning away and tracked a U.S. F-16 fighter with radar until the American warplane retaliated with a missile.

U.S. ships and planes fired 44 cruise missiles in less than 24 hours on Tuesday in two waves of attacks on air defence targets in southern Iraq to punish Saddam for a weekend military drive into a Western-protected northern safe haven for Kurds.
Pentagon officials denied Iraqi claims on Wednesday that the United States had fired a third volley of missiles at military and civilian facilities in the Baghdad area.

Clinton said Iraq withdrew its forces from the Kurdish area at least for the time being. The allies set up the northern safe haven, and another one in the south, after ousting Iraqi invasion forces from Kuwait in 1991.

"The situation in northern Iraq seems to have changed," Clinton said. "There has been a withdrawal of the (Iraqi) forces, a dispersal of the forces, but it's too soon to say that this is permanent or that further action will not be taken."
Clinton said the U.S. attacks on air defence targets in the south left Saddam "strategically worse off than he was before these strikes began."
One key goal of the U.S. action was to make it harder for Baghdad to lunge at oil-producing neighbours such as Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, Defence Secretary William Perry said.

"Our concern is that if (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein is emboldened by what he would see as a success in the north, he might strike out in areas which are of greater strategic importance to him, as well as to us, in the south," he said.
Clinton rejected suggestions that disagreements with allies, particulary France, over the missile strikes had killed the broad, U.S.-led international coalition that won the Gulf war.

"I don't think its dead," Clinton replied to a reporter who used that term. "I think quite to the contrary. We have received good support from the British. The prime minister of Canada called me last night. The German chancellor issued a strong statement ... I think things are on track."
France declined to join in patrolling a newly expanded part of the southern zone that the United States and Britain put off limits to Iraqi aircraft in retaliation for Saddam's strike at the Kurds.
The U.S. State Department said it was assessing a Turkish plan to create a security cordon inside northern Iraq to curtail Kurdish separatist activity along the border between the Turkey and Iraq.

A poll released on Wednesday showed that four out of five Americans approved of the missile attack on Iraq, but most did not expect it to stop Saddam from further violating terms of the Gulf war ceasefire.
Nearly three-quarters of the 515 adults interviewed approved of Clinton's handling of the situation, according to the ABC News poll completed before the second missile wave.

Retired Army Gen. Colin Powell, a popular Republican who was the U.S. military's top officer during the Gulf war, praised Clinton and voiced disappointment with reaction from the coalition that won the war.

"I think the president did exactly the right thing," Powell said in a CNN interview. "I must say I am a little disappointed that we didn't get the level of support that I would have expected and that we have seen in the past."
